subject: Mass Media / Mass Communication (Code: 318)
past_paper_reference: CUET UG Mass Media Past Papers (2022-2024)

questions.question: When a communicator says 'yes' while simultaneously nodding their head up and down, how does the non-verbal gesture function in relation to the spoken word?
options: A) It reinforces (or complements) the verbal message
B) It contradicts the verbal message
C) It substitutes the verbal message
D) It creates psychological noise
questions.explanation: Non-verbal cues can reinforce, complement, accent, contradict, or substitute verbal communication; nodding while saying 'yes' reinforces and confirms the statement.

questions.question: The cognitive tendency of an audience member to interpret a message in a manner that aligns with their pre-existing beliefs, attitudes, and biases while ignoring contradictory facts is called:
options: A) Selective Attention
B) Selective Perception
C) Selective Retention
D) Selective Exposure
questions.explanation: Selective perception is the psychological screening filter where individuals interpret messages through the lens of their existing values and preconceptions.

questions.question: In David Berlo's influential 1960 communication framework, what do the letters in the 'SMCR' model stand for?
options: A) Speaker, Medium, Code, Response
B) Sender, Motion, Camera, Resolution
C) Source, Message, Channel, Receiver
D) Signal, Modulation, Carrier, Relay
questions.explanation: Berlo's SMCR model outlines four essential components: Source (encoder), Message, Channel (the five senses), and Receiver (decoder).

questions.question: In mass communication theory, the process by which news editors filter, select, and decide which stories are published and which are discarded is known as:
options: A) Broadcasting
B) Narrowcasting
C) Crowdsourcing
D) Gatekeeping
questions.explanation: Originated by Kurt Lewin and applied to journalism by David Manning White (1950), gatekeeping is the editorial selection process determining what reaches the public.

questions.sub_topic: Hypodermic Needle / Magic Bullet Theory Assumption
questions.question: What core assumption regarding mass media audiences underpinned the early 20th-century 'Hypodermic Needle' (Magic Bullet) theory?
options: A) The audience is passive, atomized, and directly, uniformly manipulated by powerful media propaganda messages
B) The audience actively negotiates and decodes oppositional meanings from texts
C) Media effects are strictly mediated by local opinion leaders and family peers
D) The audience is completely immune to any political or commercial persuasion
questions.explanation: The Magic Bullet/Hypodermic Needle model assumed that mass media injects ideas directly into the minds of a defenseless, passive, and uniform mass public.

questions.question: In non-verbal communication studies, which of the following elements belongs to the domain of 'Paralanguage' (or vocalics)?
options: A) Hand gestures, facial smiles, and eye blinks
B) Pitch, volume, tempo, intonation, and vocal pauses
C) Physical distance between office desks
D) The physical fabric and color of business suits
questions.explanation: Paralanguage encompasses how something is said rather than what is said—vocal tone, pitch, speed, volume, cadence, and pauses.

questions.sub_topic: Uses and Gratifications Theory: Katz, Blumler, and Gurevitch (1974)
questions.question: How did Elihu Katz, Jay Blumler, and Michael Gurevitch's 'Uses and Gratifications' approach fundamentally invert traditional media effects paradigms?
options: A) It asserted that media audiences are helpless victims hypnotized by television cathode rays
B) It proved that reading newspapers permanently increases human memory retention by fifty percent
C) Instead of asking 'What do media do to people?', it asked 'What do active people do with media?', positing that audiences intentionally select media to fulfill cognitive and emotional needs
D) It eliminated all psychological considerations to treat mass communication as purely electrical engineering
questions.explanation: Uses and Gratifications shifted inquiry from passive media impact to active agency, studying why individuals choose specific media to satisfy personal identity, information, integration, and diversion needs.

questions.sub_topic: Attribution in Journalism: On the Record vs Off the Record
questions.question: When a source provides information to a journalist 'On the Record', it means:
options: A) The information cannot be published under any circumstances whatsoever
B) The reporter must pay the source a monetary consultation fee before writing
C) The quote can be used only if disguised as a fictional fairy tale
D) The journalist may quote the information and directly name the source by their official name and title in the published story
questions.explanation: 'On the record' means everything said can be quoted directly and attributed by name and job title to the source.

questions.question: In a news report, what is the 'Lead' (or Lede)?
options: A) The opening sentence or paragraph of the story that hooks the reader and summarizes the most vital facts
B) The metal weight placed on top of newspaper stacks during bicycle delivery
C) The final concluding sentence at the end of the classified advertisement section
D) The electrical wire connecting the computer to the printing press machine
questions.explanation: The lead (or lede) is the crucial opening of a news story, capturing the essence of the event and engaging reader attention.

questions.sub_topic: Press Release vs News Story Conversion
questions.question: When an editor receives a corporate press release, what professional practice must a credible newsroom follow before publishing?
options: A) Print the press release word-for-word on page one as an unedited news article
B) Fact-check the claims, cross-verify with independent sources, remove promotional puffery, and rewrite it objectively
C) Delete the name of the company and replace it with a rival competing company's name
D) Publish the document backwards to test whether readers are paying attention
questions.explanation: Professional ethics require journalists to treat press releases with skepticism, verifying claims, excising promotional PR hype, and investigating multiple viewpoints.

questions.sub_topic: Feature Story vs Hard News Writing Style
questions.question: In newspaper writing, how does the narrative style of a 'Feature Story' differ from a standard hard news report?
options: A) A feature story is written without using any vowels or punctuation marks
B) A feature story must only report mathematical arithmetic formulas without any words
C) A feature story uses descriptive, narrative, and emotional storytelling with a creative lead, focusing on human interest, depth, and character rather than strict inverted pyramid urgency
D) A feature story cannot exceed fifteen words in total length
questions.explanation: Feature writing adopts a literary, storytelling approach—employing colorful leads, scene-setting, character development, and narrative pacing to explore human experience.

questions.sub_topic: Galtung and Ruge: Proximity and Prominence News Values
questions.question: In journalistic news selection, why does a traffic accident in a reader's local neighborhood receive prominent front-page coverage, whereas an identical accident in a distant foreign country is ignored?
options: A) International telephone lines are physically incapable of transmitting traffic accident data
B) Newspaper printing presses refuse to print the names of foreign cities on front pages
C) Local reporters are legally barred from writing about international global events
D) The news value of 'Geographical and Cultural Proximity', which dictates that events closer to the audience have greater personal relevance and impact
questions.explanation: Proximity (geographical and psychological closeness) is a paramount news value; readers care deeply about events that directly touch their own immediate environment and community.

questions.sub_topic: Conflict of Interest: Paid News Practices
questions.question: The corrupt media practice of 'Paid News'—heavily condemned by the Press Council of India—occurs when:
options: A) A news organization publishes promotional political or corporate propaganda disguised as objective, independent editorial reporting in exchange for monetary payment
B) A reader pays five rupees at a morning newsstand to purchase a daily newspaper
C) A newspaper pays a fair monthly salary to an investigative reporter for writing articles
D) A foreign correspondent pays for an airline ticket to cover an international climate summit
questions.explanation: 'Paid News' is the deceptive and corrupt practice where advertising and political propaganda are passed off as legitimate news without disclosure, betraying editorial integrity.

questions.sub_topic: Second Press Commission of India (1982) Recommendations
questions.question: What major socio-political concern did the Second Press Commission of India (1978–1982, headed by Justice P.K. Goswami and Justice K.K. Mathew) address regarding newspaper ownership?
options: A) The mandatory nationalization of all print newspapers under direct Ministry of Information management
B) The growing concentration of newspaper ownership by large industrial conglomerates, recommending the delinking of the press from commercial business houses and diffusion of ownership
C) The complete prohibition of all regional language newspapers in favor of English-only publishing
D) The banning of all political election coverage sixty days prior to general parliamentary polls
questions.explanation: The Second Press Commission expressed alarm over cross-media concentration and monopoly control of the press by big industrial houses, advocating for 'delinking' and ownership diffusion to safeguard press independence.

questions.question: An advertising campaign created to promote public welfare, social awareness, and civic causes (such as polio vaccination, road safety, or anti-tobacco education) without promoting a commercial product is a:
options: A) Corporate Product Launch
B) Direct-Response Infomercial
C) Public Service Announcement (PSA) / Public Service Advertisement
D) Classified Commercial Ad
questions.explanation: Public Service Advertisements (PSAs) educate the public and stimulate civic behavior change on vital health, safety, and social welfare issues.

questions.question: In broadcast commercial advertising, what is a 'Jingle'?
options: A) A small metal coin given to consumers when they buy packaged breakfast cereal
B) A legal contract signed between the television network and the film director
C) A technical malfunction that causes the television audio to become mute
D) A short, catchy musical tune or rhyming song crafted specifically around a brand name or slogan to enhance audio memorability
questions.explanation: A jingle is a catchy musical slogan composed to lodge a brand name and message firmly in consumer auditory memory.

questions.topic: Advertising and Public Relations: Public Relations
questions.question: A comprehensive informational package provided to journalists at a press event, containing press releases, executive biographies, fact sheets, and high-resolution photographs, is called a:
options: A) Press Kit (or Media Kit)
B) Promotional Coupon
C) Billboard Poster
D) Direct Mail Catalog
questions.explanation: A press kit gathers all essential background resources, bios, data sheets, and imagery in one organized folder to assist reporters in writing accurate stories.

questions.question: In commercial advertising law, when a brand compares its product directly with a competing rival brand in a television commercial, it is legally permitted to do so provided it:
options: A) Purchases seventy percent of the rival brand's corporate equity stock shares prior to broadcasting
B) Compares verifiable, factual attributes truthfully and does not unfairly disparage, denigrate, or mislead consumers about the competitor's trademark
C) Uses animated cartoon animals to represent the rival company's chief executive officer
D) Airs the commercial exclusively between midnight and two o'clock in the morning
questions.explanation: Comparative advertising is lawful as long as comparisons are truthful, substantiable, and avoid unfair disparagement or slander of a competitor's registered goods.

questions.topic: Advertising and Public Relations: Public Relations
questions.sub_topic: Internal vs External Publics in PR
questions.question: In corporate public relations strategy, which group constitutes an organization's 'Internal Public'?
options: A) General consumers, external media journalists, and government tax regulators
B) Rival commercial competitors operating in competing international markets
C) Employees, management, staff labor unions, and board directors within the organization
D) Citizens living in foreign countries who have never heard of the organization
questions.explanation: Internal publics are those within the organizational boundary (employees, management, unions, retirees); external publics include customers, media, investors, and regulators.

questions.topic: Advertising and Public Relations: Advertising Theory
questions.sub_topic: Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs in Advertising Strategy
questions.question: When luxury automobile brands (like Mercedes-Benz or Rolls-Royce) craft aspirational advertising copy appealing to social prestige, self-worth, and elite status, which level of Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs are they targeting?
options: A) Physiological Needs (Food, Water, Warmth)
B) Safety and Security Needs (Physical Protection)
C) Basic Survival Needs (Shelter and Oxygen)
D) Esteem Needs (Status, Recognition, Self-Respect)
questions.explanation: Luxury and prestige advertising targets Maslow's Esteem Needs (status, mastery, prestige, recognition), associating ownership with self-worth and social admiration.

questions.question: What is the key visual and mechanical distinction between a 'Dolly In' and a 'Zoom In'?
options: A) A Dolly physically moves the entire camera forward through space on wheels, changing spatial depth, while a Zoom changes the optical focal length of the stationary lens
B) A Dolly rotates the camera upside down, while a Zoom turns off the camera power battery
C) A Dolly is used only on airplanes, while a Zoom is used only on submarines
D) A Dolly changes video into audio, while a Zoom changes audio into text
questions.explanation: A dolly physically wheels the camera through 3D space, shifting parallax and perspective; a zoom magnifies the image optically from a stationary camera position.

questions.question: In a television studio lighting grid, what is the purpose of placing a translucent 'Diffuser' (or Softbox) in front of a harsh key light?
options: A) To physically change the light beam from white light to invisible infrared radiation
B) To scatter the light rays, softening harsh dark shadows and producing gentle, flattering illumination on the talent's face
C) To prevent the studio lighting technician from falling asleep during the broadcast
D) To completely extinguish the electrical bulb so the studio becomes totally dark
questions.explanation: Diffusers, scrims, and softboxes scatter directional light beams, creating soft, wraparound illumination with gradual shadow transitions.

questions.question: In a television broadcast production crew, what are the typical responsibilities of a 'Production Assistant' (PA)?
options: A) Writing the supreme judicial rulings for constitutional bench court cases
B) Repairing high-voltage electrical power grid substations across municipal districts
C) Supporting the director and producer with logistics, timing logs, organizing scripts, escorting guests, and managing studio paperwork
D) Performing live musical violin solos during prime-time evening news bulletins
questions.explanation: The Production Assistant (PA) is the versatile backbone of a production crew, handling administrative duties, timing, talent coordination, and paperwork.

questions.sub_topic: Boom Microphone and Shotgun Mic Operation
questions.question: During television drama shooting, why does a boom operator position a 'Shotgun Microphone' on an overhead telescopic boom pole just outside the camera frame?
options: A) To shoot physical metallic pellets at background actors who forget their lines
B) To block studio lighting fixtures from overheating the camera operator's head
C) To measure the physical air pressure and humidity levels inside the television sound stage
D) To capture directional dialogue cleanly from actors while keeping the microphone completely invisible to the viewing audience
questions.explanation: Shotgun microphones have narrow, highly directional pickup patterns; mounted on boom poles above actors, they capture crisp dialogue without entering the shot frame.

questions.question: In cinematic and television continuity editing, what does an 'Eyeline Match' cut ensure?
options: A) It creates the illusion that a character in Shot A is looking directly at the object or person framed in Shot B by maintaining directional sightlines
B) It verifies that both actors in a scene wear identical colored contact lenses
C) It measures the physical distance between the camera operator's eyes and the viewfinder
D) It ensures that all television actors close their eyes whenever a cut occurs on screen
questions.explanation: An eyeline match preserves spatial continuity: if an actor in Shot A glances screen-right, the object of their gaze in Shot B must be positioned to match that sightline angle.

questions.question: In broadcast television economics, what distinguishes 'First-Run Syndication' from 'Off-Network Syndication'?
options: A) First-run syndication is broadcast exclusively in movie theaters, while off-network syndication is broadcast on AM radio

B) First-run syndication produces original programming sold directly to individual local stations without a network broadcast, while off-network syndication sells reruns of shows that originally aired on a major network
C) First-run syndication is prohibited from displaying commercial advertisements, while off-network syndication is fully commercial
D) First-run syndication is transmitted exclusively through analog telephone wires to hospital patient rooms
questions.explanation: First-run syndication creates original programs (e.g., Jeopardy, Wheel of Fortune) sold directly to stations market-by-market. Off-network syndication licenses reruns (e.g., Seinfeld, Friends) after network runs.

questions.question: A popular radio broadcast format where listeners dial a studio telephone number to speak live on air with the host, share opinions, or ask questions is called a:
options: A) Silent Meditation Broadcast
B) Serialized Audio Novel
C) Phone-in (or Call-in talk show)
D) Foley Sound Archive
questions.explanation: Phone-in (or call-in) shows provide real-time interactive audience participation, allowing listeners to voice opinions, seek advice, and engage with hosts.

questions.question: In audio physics, the pitch of a sound (whether it sounds high or low to the human ear) is determined by its:
options: A) Decibels (dB)
B) Bitrate (kbps)
C) Color temperature (Kelvin)
D) Frequency (measured in Hertz - Hz)
questions.explanation: Frequency (the number of sound wave cycles per second, measured in Hertz/Hz) determines perceived pitch; amplitude determines loudness (measured in Decibels/dB).

questions.question: What is the Sanskrit motto of All India Radio (Akashvani), reflecting its public service broadcasting commitment to mass enlightenment and welfare?
options: A) 'Bahujana Hitaya, Bahujana Sukhaya' (For the benefit of many, for the happiness of many)
B) 'Satyameva Jayate' (Truth Alone Triumphs)
C) 'Yogakshemam Vahamyaham' (I Carry What They Lack)
D) 'Dharmo Rakshati Rakshitah' (Dharma Protects Those Who Protect It)
questions.explanation: All India Radio's motto is 'Bahujana Hitaya, Bahujana Sukhaya' ('For the welfare of the masses, for the happiness of the masses'), inspired by Buddhist ethics.

questions.question: In radio documentary and feature production, what is the role of a 'Voice-Over' (narration)?
options: A) To shout loudly over music tracks so that listeners cannot understand the song lyrics
B) To provide narrative exposition, introduce interview clips, establish context, and bridge distinct thematic segments together
C) To imitate animal bird sounds whenever a guest speaker answers a question
D) To replace all human voices with mechanical typewriter typing sounds
questions.explanation: The voice-over narrator provides the narrative spine, offering essential exposition, thematic transitions, and context that unite interviews and ambient sound into a story.

questions.sub_topic: Dynamic vs Condenser Microphones in Radio
questions.question: Why are 'Dynamic Microphones' (like the Shure SM58 or SM7B) widely preferred for outdoor radio reporting and noisy broadcast booths compared to sensitive Condenser microphones?
options: A) They are constructed out of fragile glass crystals that melt if exposed to studio air conditioning
B) They record only high-frequency violin sounds and cannot pick up male speech
C) They are rugged, durable, do not require external phantom power, and reject excessive ambient background noise and room reflections
D) They convert spoken words into digital text printouts printed on paper rolls
questions.explanation: Dynamic mics use moving-coil mechanisms that tolerate rough handling, high sound pressure levels (SPL), and resist picking up room rumble, making them broadcast workhorses.

questions.sub_topic: Community Radio Guidelines: 2002 vs 2006 Policy Expansion
questions.question: In 2006, the Government of India revolutionized Community Radio broadcasting policy by expanding eligibility beyond educational institutions (2002 policy) to include:
options: A) Commercial foreign multinational private entertainment conglomerates
B) Armed military paramilitary regiments stationed on border checkpoints
C) Private speculative cryptocurrency trading investment funds
D) Civil society organizations, non-governmental organizations (NGOs), and community-based voluntary development groups
questions.explanation: While the 2002 policy restricted community radio to well-funded educational institutions, the historic 2006 policy opened licenses to grassroots NGOs, farming collectives, and civil society groups.

questions.question: A cinematic technique where individual inanimate drawings, clay figures, or computer models are photographed frame-by-frame and played in rapid sequence to create the illusion of movement is called:
options: A) Animation
B) Cinéma Vérité
C) Direct Cinema
D) Parallel Cinema
questions.explanation: Animation is the photographic art of bringing inanimate objects or drawings to life through sequential frame-by-frame manipulation.

questions.sub_topic: First Indian Color Film: Kisan Kanya (1937)
questions.question: Which historic 1937 motion picture, directed by Moti Gidwani and produced by Ardeshir Irani's Imperial Film Company, is recognized as India's first indigenously produced color feature film?
options: A) Mother India
B) Kisan Kanya
C) Mughal-e-Azam
D) Devdas
questions.explanation: Moti Gidwani's 'Kisan Kanya' (1937) was India's first indigenously manufactured Cinecolor feature film, dealing with the plight of an impoverished farmer.

questions.question: A camera shot that shows the scene exactly through the physical eyes of a character, replicating what they see from their exact physical vantage point, is called a:
options: A) Bird's Eye View shot
B) Master shot
C) Point-of-View (POV) shot
D) Cutaway shot
questions.explanation: A POV (Point of View) shot aligns the camera with a character's eyes, plunging the audience into subjective visual identification with that character.

questions.question: In cinematic sound design, how does 'Diegetic Sound' differ from 'Non-Diegetic Sound'?
options: A) Diegetic sound is recorded exclusively on analog wax cylinders, while non-diegetic sound is digital
B) Diegetic sound can only be heard by children under ten years old, while non-diegetic sound is heard by adults
C) Diegetic sound is completely silent, while non-diegetic sound is deafening white noise

D) Diegetic sound originates within the narrative world of the film (heard by characters, e.g., dialogue or radio in a car), while non-diegetic sound exists outside the story world (heard only by the audience, e.g., musical background score)
questions.explanation: Diegetic sound belongs to the film's diegesis (characters can hear it: dialogue, footsteps, cars); non-diegetic sound is added for the audience (voiceover commentary, background score).

questions.question: Which set of aesthetic conventions characterized the Italian Neorealist film movement that emerged in post-World War II Italy (exemplified by Roberto Rossellini and Vittorio De Sica)?
options: A) Extensive on-location shooting, use of non-professional actors, natural lighting, and focus on the daily economic struggles of the working poor
B) Elaborate studio soundstages, glamorous movie stars, lavish costumes, and escapist romantic melodramas
C) Surreal painted sets, distorted perspectives, and extreme chiaroscuro horror lighting
D) High-budget computer-generated animation featuring intergalactic space battles
questions.explanation: Italian Neorealism emerged from post-war wreckage, rejecting fascist studio escapism in favor of real Roman streets, non-actors, and raw socio-economic realism.

questions.sub_topic: Auteur Theory Origins: Cahiers du Cinéma (1950s)
questions.question: In the influential French film journal 'Cahiers du Cinéma', what controversial thesis did young critic François Truffaut champion in his 1954 manifesto 'A Certain Tendency in the French Cinema'?
options: A) That all motion picture theaters must be legally closed on Sundays to conserve electrical energy
B) La politique des Auteurs: asserting that great cinema arises from directors who imprint their personal thematic and visual worldview onto the film, rebelling against dry literary screenwriters
C) That motion pictures should eliminate human actors and rely entirely on hand-drawn puppet cartoons
D) That movie directors should have zero control over filmmaking, surrendering all choices to theater owners
questions.explanation: Truffaut's essay attacked the French 'Tradition of Quality' (dry literary adaptations), championing the director as the true visionary auteur whose visual signature elevates cinema to high art.

questions.question: An individual on a social media platform who has built a substantial, loyal following and has the credibility to influence their audience's opinions and purchasing decisions is an:
options: A) Adjudicator
B) Underwriter
C) Influencer
D) Arbitrator
questions.explanation: Social media influencers leverage their niche authority, charisma, and content to shape follower attitudes, consumer behaviors, and trends.

questions.question: According to ethical and secure digital citizenship guidelines, what is the best practice for protecting one's social media accounts against unauthorized hacking?
options: A) Using one's own first name and birth year as the password for every single digital account
B) Sharing one's login password publicly in the biography section of their social media profile
C) Writing one's account password on a sticky note attached to a public library computer monitor
D) Using strong, unique alphanumeric passwords with special characters and enabling Two-Factor Authentication (2FA)
questions.explanation: Digital hygiene mandates strong unique passwords and multi-factor authentication (2FA) to safeguard online identities from credential stuffing and breaches.

questions.question: What is the defining technical feature of 'Stories' (or ephemeral content) popularized by Snapchat and Instagram?
options: A) The posted photos or short video clips disappear automatically after 24 hours unless saved as highlights
B) The content is printed on paper and mailed to all followers via the national postal service
C) The video can only be viewed if the user pays five hundred dollars per second of playback
D) The photos remain permanently locked inside the smartphone battery storage unit
questions.explanation: Ephemeral content (Stories) vanishes after 24 hours, encouraging casual, spontaneous, real-time sharing without cluttering a permanent profile grid.

questions.sub_topic: FOMO and Social Media Comparison Culture
questions.question: Sociological studies on Instagram usage indicate that excessive consumption of heavily curated, filtered lifestyle posts frequently leads young users to experience:
options: A) An instantaneous surge in physical muscle strength and mathematical calculation speed
B) Unfavorable social comparison, lower self-esteem, and body image dissatisfaction
C) The permanent loss of the ability to speak one's native mother tongue
D) A sudden profound desire to abandon electricity and live in medieval castles
questions.explanation: Curated highlight reels on visual social media promote upward social comparison, where users benchmark their real messy lives against idealized digital facades, fueling anxiety.

questions.question: What is the primary editorial and algorithmic objective of sensationalist 'Clickbait' headlines on social news feeds?
options: A) To provide a calm, comprehensive, objective academic summary of peer-reviewed research papers
B) To convince users to turn off their mobile phones and read classical literature in public libraries
C) To exploit an information gap or evoke extreme curiosity and emotional shock to manipulate users into clicking, generating ad revenue and algorithmic impressions
D) To teach software engineers how to write computer programming code in C++
questions.explanation: Clickbait headlines use sensationalism, hyperbole, and curiosity gaps ('You Won't Believe What Happened Next!') to bait clicks, monetizing attention regardless of actual content value.

questions.topic: Social Media: Cyber Crimes and Law
questions.sub_topic: Section 66A of IT Act (Shreya Singhal Case, 2015)
questions.question: In the landmark freedom of speech ruling 'Shreya Singhal v. Union of India' (2015), why did the Supreme Court strike down Section 66A of the Information Technology Act, 2000?
options: A) The legislation failed to provide free laptop computers to high school students in rural districts
B) The IT Act had not been translated into the English language prior to parliamentary approval
C) The Supreme Court declared that social media platforms are completely immune from all national laws
D) It was unconstitutionally vague, overbroad, and chilled free speech by criminalizing any online message deemed 'offensive' or 'annoying' without reasonable nexus to Article 19(2)
questions.explanation: The Supreme Court struck down Section 66A for vagueness and overbreadth, ruling that mere 'annoyance' or 'inconvenience' cannot be criminalized under Article 19(2) free speech protections.

questions.question: A specialized web-based software program that crawls the internet, indexes web pages, and retrieves relevant results based on user search queries (exemplified by Google) is a:
options: A) Search Engine
B) Word Processor
C) Spreadsheet Calculator
D) Video Game Console
questions.explanation: Search engines use automated web crawlers (spiders) to index billions of pages, using ranking algorithms to deliver relevant links matching user keyword queries.

questions.question: In modern digital media production, what is the primary operational advantage of 'Cloud Storage' and computing (such as Google Drive or Dropbox)?
options: A) It physically stores computer memory drives inside high-altitude rain clouds in the sky
B) It allows media professionals to store, edit, and access massive video and audio files collaboratively from any internet-connected device worldwide
C) It eliminates the need for computer monitors and displays images on water vapor
D) It permanently deletes all files if the weather becomes sunny and hot
questions.explanation: Cloud computing enables remote data storage and compute over the internet, facilitating seamless cross-border collaboration, automated backups, and global file access.

questions.question: During a breaking news crisis, parliamentary budget presentation, or sporting championship, what digital news format publishes bite-sized, time-stamped text and video updates in real time on a single webpage?
options: A) Monthly Printed Magazine
B) Annual Financial Ledger
C) Live Blog (or Rolling News Page)
D) Academic Monograph
questions.explanation: Live blogs provide real-time, chronological timestamped feeds of bite-sized updates, multimedia clips, and social posts during fast-moving breaking news events.

questions.question: What is the defining philosophy of 'Open-Source Software' (such as Linux, Audacity, or OBS Studio) widely used by digital content creators?
options: A) The software can only be operated outdoors under an open sky without a roof
B) Users are legally required to purchase a fifty-thousand-dollar software license every month
C) The software permanently locks computer screens after thirty seconds of use
D) The source code is publicly accessible, allowing anyone to inspect, modify, enhance, and freely distribute the software without paying proprietary licensing fees
questions.explanation: Open-source software provides transparent source code under licenses (GPL, MIT) encouraging collaboration, peer auditing, free distribution, and user community enhancement.

questions.topic: New Media: Digital Literacy and Ethics
questions.question: In digital politics and public relations, what is an 'Astroturfing' campaign?
options: A) A deceptive public relations practice that artificially manufactures the illusion of widespread, spontaneous grassroots citizen support using fake accounts, bots, and paid shills
B) A municipal sports initiative to replace dirt playing fields with artificial green synthetic grass
C) A genuine non-profit charity campaign organized entirely by volunteers without corporate funding
D) A space exploration program that launches botanical seed experiments into Earth's orbit
questions.explanation: Astroturfing creates synthetic, manufactured public support ('fake grassroots') funded by political or corporate interests to deceptively sway public opinion and algorithms.

questions.topic: New Media: Cyber Law and Privacy
questions.sub_topic: Cookies and Digital Tracking: First-Party vs Third-Party
questions.question: In digital web architecture and advertising, what is the critical technical and privacy difference between a 'First-Party Cookie' and a 'Third-Party Cookie'?
options: A) First-party cookies are baked in commercial ovens, while third-party cookies are made out of chocolate
B) First-party cookies can only store mathematical numbers, while third-party cookies store spoken audio

C) A first-party cookie is created and stored by the website the user directly visits (remembering login and cart items), whereas a third-party cookie is set by an external tracking/advertising domain to track user browsing history across multiple unrelated websites
D) First-party cookies require government passports, while third-party cookies are completely illegal everywhere
questions.explanation: First-party cookies manage site functionality (logins, carts) directly on the host site. Third-party cookies track users cross-site across domains for behavioral profiling and targeted advertising.
